generatedProse.concept-context: In practice, a critical edge comes from controlling what a source does in your writing, not from stacking references. The 'voices' technique fits any field: open a paragraph in your own voice with its point, bring in sources to support or qualify it, then close in your voice with what you make of them. The language of criticality, which weighs and qualifies rather than simply reports, signals where you are judging the evidence rather than passing it on.
generatedProse.worked-example:
Consider two students using the same source, a study reporting a strong result, in a paragraph of their own.

{{learner-a}} writes: 'Rahman (2019) found a large effect. This shows the approach works.' The source is cited correctly, but it is simply reported and then accepted. The paragraph has no voice of its own: it passes on the finding and takes its conclusion as settled. This is reporting, not arguing.

{{learner-b}} writes instead: 'The case is not yet settled. Rahman (2019) reports a large effect. But the single setting limits how far it generalises.' The paragraph opens and closes in {{learner-b}}'s own voice. The source supports a point rather than making it. The language of criticality, weighing and qualifying, flags the judgement.

Both students used the same source accurately. Only {{learner-b}} made it serve an argument, and showed the reader where the criticism was happening.
generatedProse.summary: A critical edge comes from controlling what a source does in your writing. The 'voices' technique frames each paragraph in your own voice and uses sources to serve its point, while the language of criticality signals where you are weighing rather than reporting. You can now integrate a source this way, flag your criticality, and tell writing that advances an argument from writing that only reports. With conventions recognised, learned and put to work, you can write as a member of your discipline.

check.body: In the worked example, what made {{learner-b}}'s paragraph read as an argument rather than a report?

items.text: It framed the point in {{learner-b}}'s own voice and used the language of criticality to weigh the source.
It accepted the finding without question.

feedback.correct: That's right. Own-voice framing and the language of criticality turned the source into support for an argument.
feedback.incorrectNotFinal: Not quite. Look at how {{learner-b}} framed and weighed the source.
feedback.incorrectFinal: {{learner-b}}'s paragraph read as an argument because it was framed in their own voice and used the language of criticality to weigh the source, not because it quoted more or dropped the citation.
